solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

parts.note: the single letter R sits at the centre of the numeral three

explanation.surface: A cryptic shorthand that looks like a label or a grid reference: a letter beside a number.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as THREE'S CORE: the middle letter of THREE is R, which is all the wordplay the clue prints.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so three of them make sixty, an old way of counting years.

clue.text: Textbook in purse carried by child

indicators.note: carried by says the purse word is held inside the child word, as a child might carry something

parts.note: a son is a child
a pot is the prize money or kitty, a purse in a contest

explanation.surface: A schoolbook stuffed into a purse that a youngster is carrying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Textbook' is the definition in its adjective sense, as in a textbook example.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done by the book, exactly as it should be, is perfectly accurate or exact.

clue.text: Wave like a comedienne?

parts.note: Jo Brand is a British comedienne
the suffix -ish means like or somewhat

explanation.surface: Waving about in the manner of a stand-up comic.
explanation.walkthrough: Jo Brand is a well-known British stand-up comedian; -ISH added to her name gives 'like Brand'.
explanation.definitionFit: To flourish something, such as a sword, is to wave it about menacingly.

clue.text: One of backroom staff delivered bubbly — well I never!

indicators.note: delivered means spoken, so the words are judged by how they sound when uttered

parts.note: bubbly is fizzy and well I never is the exclamation oh

explanation.surface: A member of the support team brought sparkling wine, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: FIZZY plus O, said together, gives the sound of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A sports team's physiotherapist works behind the scenes treating injured players.

clue.text: Greatest challenge in running old bar

definitions.meaning: the 26-mile road race is the longest standard event a runner faces
The former British name of the chocolate bar now sold as Snickers

explanation.surface: The hardest test of running could be an ancient bar-room session.
explanation.definitionFit: The 26-mile race is the toughest standard running event, and also an old British name for the Snickers bar.

clue.text: Sort of boxing match, say

indicators.note: say means the word is to be heard rather than written

parts.note: a tie is a match, as in a cup tie

explanation.surface: A kind of boxing bout.
explanation.walkthrough: TIE and the answer sound alike.
explanation.definitionFit: Muay Thai is the kickboxing style from Thailand, often just called Thai boxing.

clue.text: Mobile phone or one going nowhere?

indicators.note: mobile means moving about, so these letters are set in motion into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone stuck on their mobile phone, getting nowhere in life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like part of 'mobile phone', but it is the anagram signal for PHONE OR.
explanation.definitionFit: A person or horse with no chance of success is a hopeless case who will get nowhere.

clue.text: OK to anger?

parts.note: the words to anger are what you get if you shake up the letters of no great, so this phrase describes them

explanation.surface: Is it all right to make someone cross?
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: NO GREAT 'shakes', that is rearranged, makes TO ANGER, the clue's own words.
explanation.definitionFit: Something only passable, not especially good, is middling or mediocre.

clue.text: Try to hold the broom?

indicators.note: to hold says the first word grips the second inside it

parts.note: to hear a case is to try it in court

explanation.surface: An attempt to grasp a sweeping brush.
explanation.walkthrough: A judge hears, that is tries, a case. The question mark is there because broom here is the shrub, and the answer is a related moorland shrub that was also bound into brooms.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are small flowering shrubs of heath and moor, and heather twigs were once tied into brooms.

clue.text: Return to post and check report

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
a statement is a report or account

explanation.surface: Coming back to work and checking a report.
explanation.definitionFit: Restoring someone to the job they held before is giving them their old position back.

clue.text: His scrambled egg isn't full of soldiers

indicators.note: full of says the scrambled letters hold the soldiers inside them
scrambled means mixed up, as eggs are, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, RE, are soldiers

explanation.surface: A man's scrambled egg is missing its toast fingers, called soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His' is the plural of 'hi', a hello. 'full of' puts RE inside GETINGS, the letters of EGG ISN'T mixed up. Soldiers are also toast strips for dipping in eggs, a British breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Each hi is a word of welcome, so several of them are salutations.

clue.text: Adult 'freedom' — Independent 'story'

parts.note: A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
lib is short for liberation, freedom

explanation.surface: An adult's freedom set against the Independent newspaper's story.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse claiming you were elsewhere is a story told to escape blame.

clue.text: German city fortress enlists guards

indicators.note: guards says the words around protect a run of letters held within them

explanation.surface: A German stronghold signs up sentries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'guards' looks like the noun, but it is the verb: the two words hold the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the industrial city in the Ruhr, North Rhine-Westphalia.

clue.text: Is alternative title 'We show where t = x'?

parts.note: other means alternative, as in the other option
Ms is a title for a woman

explanation.surface: Asking whether a book's other name is a maths statement.
explanation.walkthrough: t stands for temperature: the lines on a weather map joining places where the temperature equals some value x.
explanation.definitionFit: These map contours link points of equal temperature, so along each one temperature has a single value.

clue.text: Lively lecture

definitions.meaning: boisterous and full of high spirits
a telling-off, a severe scolding, in British informal use

explanation.definitionFit: The word means exuberantly jolly, and in British slang a stern dressing-down.

clue.text: Unwarranted award out of play?

indicators.note: out of play reads as in touch, so the award is placed within the off-field strip that stops play

parts.note: touch is the area beyond the touchlines in rugby or football, where the ball is dead
the OM, Order of Merit, is an award

explanation.surface: An undeserved prize given away while the game was stopped.
explanation.walkthrough: A ball out of play has gone 'into touch', the strip beside a rugby or football pitch, so the award sits in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Excessive, beyond what is called for, so not justified.

clue.text: North America's pottery in America, unexpectedly

indicators.note: in places the first group inside the letters for the country

parts.note: US is short for the United States, America
ware is pottery, as in earthenware

explanation.surface: A continent's ceramics turn up in the United States out of the blue.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken off guard, by surprise, without warning.

clue.text: Golf and old Ford are focuses of interest

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Ford Anglia was a British car of the 1950s and 60s

explanation.surface: A round of golf and a vintage car hold people's attention.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ford Anglia was a small British family car, last made in 1967.
explanation.definitionFit: A ganglion is figuratively a centre of activity or energy, so the plural means hubs of attention.

clue.text: One playing around starts to like more laughing

indicators.note: around says the player wraps the beginning of the next word

parts.note: a gigger is one who plays gigs

indicators.note: starts to means the opening letters of the word that follows are taken

explanation.surface: A philanderer finds himself starting to enjoy himself more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One playing around' suggests a philanderer, but 'around' is the container signal. 'starts to' takes LI, the first two letters of 'like'.
explanation.definitionFit: Giggly means prone to laughter, so the comparative form means given to more chuckling.

clue.text: Braying from male — what a player!

parts.note: he is the male pronoun
eh is an exclamation meaning what?
a wing is a player on the flank, in rugby or football

explanation.surface: Loud boasting from a man showing off his sporting talent.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey's cry is a bray, and the imitative word for it describes the noise.

clue.text: Lag using some satin material

indicators.note: using some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone falling behind by making do with a bit of silky fabric.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lag' is not falling behind but a convict, as in old lag.
explanation.definitionFit: A lag is British slang for a convict, someone serving time in prison.

clue.text: Pilot runs into nightclub

indicators.note: into says the runs letter is put inside the club word

parts.note: a dive is a seedy nightclub or bar
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: An airline captain dashes into a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pilot' is a verb here, to steer.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer a vehicle or guide a course is to be at the controls.

clue.text: Want love? This is not needed

parts.note: dear is a term of endearment like love

indicators.note: not needed says the word is is dropped from the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone asking whether they want love, and being told it is unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not needed' removes IS from THIS, leaving TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Want here is a noun meaning lack, a scarcity of something.

clue.text: Rather informal family lawyer

parts.note: kin is family
a DA is a district attorney, a US prosecuting lawyer

explanation.surface: A lawyer in the family who is fairly casual.
explanation.definitionFit: This slang contraction of kind of means somewhat or sort of in casual speech.

clue.text: Duck on English river

parts.note: a duck is a score of zero in cricket

explanation.surface: A duck swimming on a river in England.
explanation.definitionFit: The great African waterway flowing north through Egypt to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Outbreak of leukemia around western US city

indicators.note: around says the reshuffled letters go round the western letter
an outbreak breaks the letters apart so they reassemble in another order

explanation.surface: An epidemic of blood cancer spreading round a city in the American West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outbreak of' rearranges LEUKEMIA (the US spelling) into MILAUKEE, and 'around' puts that about W.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the largest city in Wisconsin, on Lake Michigan.

clue.text: It may be used to remove sound?

definitions.text: It may be used to remove
definitions.meaning: a liquid that dissolves things, used to lift off stains or paint
financially sound, able to pay all debts

explanation.definitionFit: The word names a dissolving liquid used in cleaning, and also describes a business able to meet its debts.

clue.text: Old colour's gone

parts.note: ex means former or old, as in ex-wife
a tinct is a tint or colour

explanation.surface: An old shade has faded away.
explanation.definitionFit: A species that has died out completely has gone for ever.
